Who bills you and who sets the value

Two parish offices split the work. The East Baton Rouge Parish Assessor puts a value on your house. The Parish Sheriff, who doubles as tax collector, sends the notice and receives the money. The Sheriff has no say in the amount: your bill is the assessed value times the millage rates attached to your property, and voters in the parish approve the millages.

Baton Rouge is a consolidated city-parish, so one tax notice can carry parish levies, city levies and several district charges. Every city in the parish except Central collects its city taxes on the same notice, which includes Baton Rouge, Baker and Zachary.

  • Assessor (values the property): City Hall, Room 126, phone (225) 389-3920.
  • Sheriff, Tax Department (bills and collects): City Hall, 2nd Floor, 222 Saint Louis Street, Room 238; (225) 389-4810.
  • Walk-in counter at the Sheriff's tax office is staffed weekdays from 8:30 AM until 4:30 PM.

The Assessor's office does not accept payment. Send it to the Sheriff.

Baton Rouge in brief

The state capital lies roughly 79 miles from New Orleans, along the Mississippi's eastern shore. The 2020 census counted 227,470 people in the city, the second-largest in the state, and 870,569 in the Greater Baton Rouge metro. Louisiana State University and Southern University are both based here, and state government and the river port keep housing demand steady.

Settlers built on the Istrouma Bluff, the earliest natural high ground north of the delta, to stay clear of seasonal river flooding. Flood risk is still a question buyers ask.

How a Baton Rouge home is assessed

The assessor estimates market value, studies sales of similar homes nearby, and assesses a residential property at 10% of that value. Commercial buildings are assessed at 15% of market value, which is why a rental-heavy block can show a different tax pattern from an owner-occupied one.

Millage also varies by location within the parish. Property inside city limits usually shares one rate, apart from the downtown development district, the levee district and the Comite River Diversion Canal district. Property outside the city can carry extra millages for fire protection, road lighting, garbage and the canal. Your own notice shows exactly which rates apply to your parcel.

Homestead exemption in East Baton Rouge Parish

For the house you own and live in, the first $75,000 of market value, or $7,500 assessed, is free of parish tax. City taxes and fire and crime district fees are not reduced.

The exemption is worth roughly $750 to $800 a year, depending on assessed value and the millage in your area. To qualify, you need to own the home and live in it by December 31 of the tax year. Renewal is automatic until the title changes.

Extra relief exists for some owners:

  • An owner with a service-connected disability rating of 50% through 69% gets an additional $2,500 of assessed value exempt, and 70% through 99% gets $4,500. A 100% rating exempts the full assessed value from parish tax, though city taxes and fees stay on the bill.
  • A special assessment level holds the assessed value steady for owners 65 or older who live in the house, have the homestead exemption, and report adjusted gross income of no more than $102,700.

Baton Rouge property tax dates

Each tax year opens January 1 and closes with the December 31 payment deadline.

Yearly dates for East Baton Rouge Parish owners
DateWhat happens
January 1Property is assessed for condition and ownership as of this date
April 1Businesses must turn in self-reporting forms for personal property
August 15 to September 15The roll can be inspected by the public for 15 days; the Advocate prints the exact dates
November 15Louisiana Tax Commission certifies the roll; the Sheriff mails notices shortly after, usually the last week of November
December 31Taxes due; delinquent after this date, with interest at 1% per month

A postmark proves timely mailing only if the U.S. Postal Service actually canceled the envelope.

How to challenge a Baton Rouge assessment

Review the value while the books are open, then take the dispute to the Metro Council sitting as the board of review. During the 15-calendar-day inspection window the assessor's staff can discuss discrepancies in value. A call to the Assessor after August 1 will get you that year's open dates.

Whichever way the Metro Council rules, the owner or the assessor can take the case to the Louisiana Tax Commission. Board of review dates shift annually, so phone the Assessor for this year's.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax at a Baton Rouge closing

Taxes get settled, not paid, when a Baton Rouge house closes. The collector never splits a bill between buyer and seller, so any arrangement between them is private. Whatever is unpaid, plus interest and fees, remains attached to the property.

State law bills the person who held the property on January 1. A buyer who closes later may find the notice still addressed to the previous owner, and it is the buyer's job to check what is owed. The Sheriff can issue a tax certificate showing taxes are paid, and an abstract of title with title insurance is advised.

  • Before signing a contract, get the balance from the Sheriff's Tax Office, (225) 389-4810.
  • When a lender escrows your taxes, request proof that it paid. Duplicate payments are not reversed, because the first one received is the one posted.
  • After the title changes, the new owner signs a new homestead application along with the closing papers.

Delinquency rules recently changed. Beginning January 1, 2026, Louisiana tax collectors auction a tax lien certificate each year instead of the property itself. Treat any delinquent balance as urgent, and ask the Sheriff how the process works now.

Selling with back taxes owed

You can sell a house that has tax due, provided the balance is paid out of the proceeds when the title company closes. Know your numbers before you list or take an offer and nothing catches you off guard at the table.

Falling behind usually has an ordinary cause: a homestead exemption that lapsed after an inheritance, a mailing address nobody updated so notices went to a relative, or an escrow account that was never funded. If you are behind, phone the Sheriff first. After that, a title company or attorney can walk you through the payoff.

With a cash sale there is no lender underwriting, so an unpaid balance simply becomes another line on the settlement statement. Get the figure from the Sheriff's Tax Office, pass it to whoever is closing, and afterward confirm the new owner's name is on the tax roll.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property tax to in Baton Rouge?

You pay the East Baton Rouge Parish Sheriff, who is the tax collector. You can pay online through the link on the Sheriff's site, mail the payment with the stub, or pay in person at City Hall, 2nd Floor, 222 Saint Louis Street, Room 238, from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays. The Assessor's Office does not accept payment.

When are Baton Rouge property taxes due?

Taxes are due by December 31 each year and are delinquent after that date, with interest at 1% per month. The Sheriff usually mails notices during the last week of November.

Does the Baton Rouge homestead exemption lower my city tax?

No. The exemption removes parish tax on the first $75,000 of market value ($7,500 assessed), but it does not apply to city taxes or to fire and crime district fees.

Do buyer and seller split the tax bill at a Baton Rouge closing?

The tax collector does not prorate between buyer and seller. Any sharing of the bill is a private arrangement handled at closing, and the full bill remains owed to the Sheriff until paid.

How do I appeal my Baton Rouge assessment?

Review the assessment during the open-roll period, which runs 15 calendar days between August 15 and September 15, then bring the complaint to the Metro Council sitting as the board of review. Either side can then appeal to the Louisiana Tax Commission.

Caddo or Bossier: which parish bills you

Most Shreveport houses are billed by Caddo Parish, since the city is the Caddo Parish seat. Part of the city extends along the west bank of the Red River into Bossier Parish, though, and a house on that side deals with the Bossier Parish assessor and tax collector instead. Check which parish your parcel is in before you go looking for a bill.

A Shreveport mailing address can also belong to a house in one of the small places outside the city, such as Bethany, Dixie, Keithville or Mira. That can change the tax bill, so read the parcel record instead of trusting the postal name.

The city had 187,593 residents in the 2020 census, and the 2024 estimate is 176,578, below the 1980 high of 206,989. The median home was built in 1973, so many houses are fifty years old or more.

Where to look up or pay your property tax

Both Caddo offices share one building: 501 Texas Street in downtown Shreveport. The Assessor is in Room 102, and the Sheriff's tax division is in Room 101.

OfficeWhat it doesContact
Caddo Parish AssessorValues property, handles homestead exemption filings501 Texas Street, Room 102, 318.226.6704, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. weekdays
Caddo Parish Sheriff, Tax DivisionBills and collects the tax501 Texas Street, Room 101, (318) 675-2170

The Assessor's website offers a free property search by owner name, section, township and range, or subdivision, with GIS maps. A day pass for deeper searches costs $10, and a professional subscription is $35 a month.

The Sheriff's site takes payments online, and online tax payments post the same day until 11:59 p.m. It also has a pre-payment program and links to delinquent properties and sheriff sales.

Due dates and late penalties

The deadline is December 31. After that, 1% interest is added for every month the tax sits unpaid. The parish collector mails a bill each December that shows the millages and the total due.

Leave it long enough and the collector can put the house up at a tax sale. The former owner then has three years to buy it back. Three years sounds generous, but interest and costs pile up the whole time, so if a delinquency notice arrives, call the Sheriff's tax division that same week.

For an exact interest or fee figure, ask the office for a payoff instead of estimating one. A written payoff is also what a title company needs for a sale.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How homes are assessed and how to appeal

A Shreveport house is taxed on 10% of its fair market value. The ratios are 15% for commercial property and 25% for public service property. If you think the value is wrong, your recourse is the local Board of Review.

Assessment rolls are generally open to the public from August 15 to September 15. Use those weeks to pull your parcel card and set it beside sales of similar houses near you.

  • Check the square footage, bedroom count and year built on the parcel card.
  • Look for exemptions you may have missed.
  • Ask the Assessor how to file with the Board of Review.

Homestead exemption

The homestead exemption applies to $7,500 of assessed value, which is $75,000 of fair market value. In Caddo, homeowners can apply for it online through the parcel card on the Assessor's property search. Owners 65 and older should ask the Assessor about the special assessment freeze.

If you are selling, remember that a buyer has to claim the exemption on their own once they own and live in the house. Do not promise a buyer your current bill.

Roof, heat and the age of the house

Shreveport has a humid subtropical climate, and severe thunderstorms, hail, damaging winds and tornadoes are part of spring and summer. About 91 days a year top 90 degrees. That mix is hard on roofs and cooling systems, and buyers' inspectors tend to look first at the roof, the HVAC unit, the plumbing and the electrical panel.

  • Keep roof receipts and any storm claim paperwork.
  • Note the age of your air conditioner.
  • Write down any past leaks so the disclosure you give is accurate.

The western and northern parts of the city are low and close to the river, so a flood-zone check matters more there than for houses on higher ground.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens to the tax when you sell

Any unpaid tax comes out of your sale proceeds through the title company. La. R.S. 9:2721 also asks the deed to identify who is responsible for the taxes and where notices should be mailed, a detail people skip when closing is rushed.

Ask the Sheriff for a current payoff before closing day. If the sale falls in November or December, the new bill may already be on its way, so agree in writing who covers the year.

The transfer is made by authentic act or act under private signature, and it reaches third persons only once recorded. A Caddo Parish parcel is recorded with the parish clerk of court.

Ask your closing agent who will carry the act to the clerk and when. Recording on the closing date keeps the public record current and lets the buyer's first bill go to the right address.

What to bring when you call or visit

Both offices work faster when you arrive with the right details. Bring your parcel number or owner name, the address as it appears on your deed, and a photo ID. If you are selling for someone else, bring whatever shows you have authority to act, such as succession papers.

At the Assessor's office, Room 102, ask about the homestead exemption, any special assessment freeze for owners 65 and older, and how to reach the Board of Review. At the Sheriff's tax division, Room 101, ask for a payoff, the status of the current year and whether any earlier year is open.

If you cannot make it downtown, the Assessor's online search and the Sheriff's online payment page cover most routine questions without a trip. Heirs who live out of town can use both from anywhere.

Selling with tax owed: the order of work

A house with a past-due bill can still sell, and the steps are short.

  1. Confirm the parish. A parcel on the Bossier side has a different assessor and collector.
  2. Pull the parcel record from the Assessor's search and check the facts on it.
  3. Get a written payoff from the Sheriff's tax division at 501 Texas Street, Room 101.
  4. Give the payoff to your title company so it can pay the balance from your proceeds.
  5. Record the sale with the Caddo Parish clerk of court.

A cash buyer can close on that same path without waiting for a lender, which helps when a delinquency notice has a date on it.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is Shreveport in Caddo or Bossier Parish?

Most of Shreveport is in Caddo Parish, which it serves as parish seat. Parts of the city extend into Bossier Parish.

When is Shreveport property tax due?

Property tax is due December 31, and 1% interest per month applies after that. Ask the Caddo Sheriff's tax division for the exact payoff.

How do I pay Caddo Parish property tax?

You can pay online through the Caddo Sheriff's site, where online payments post the same day until 11:59 p.m. You can also visit 501 Texas Street, Room 101.

What is the Louisiana homestead exemption?

The exemption covers $7,500 of assessed value, which is $75,000 of fair market value. Caddo owners can apply through the Assessor's online property search.

Can I sell my Shreveport house if I owe tax?

Yes. The unpaid tax is paid out of the sale proceeds, and the title company needs a payoff figure from the Sheriff.

Lafayette housing and drainage

Lafayette is a city of about 121,000 people in the Acadiana region of south Louisiana, and the 2020 census put it at 121,374, fourth largest in the state. It sits on the Vermilion River about 59 miles from Baton Rouge and 135 miles from New Orleans, on prairie terrace that stands higher than the wetlands to the south and west. Hospitals, the university and energy work keep housing demand fairly steady, though a slump in oil activity can slow it.

Flooding is mostly a flash-flood issue here. Water drains through natural coulees, including Isaac Verot Coulee, Coulee Mine, Coulee des Poches and Coulee Ile des Cannes, all running to the Vermilion. If your lot backs onto a coulee, expect buyers to ask about drainage and flood insurance, and check the flood zone for your specific address before you list.

Older houses with a worn roof or a failing air conditioner can frighten off financed buyers, since lenders and appraisers flag those items. Some sellers repair first and others sell as-is. Either way, know what an inspector will find.

Who to call

OfficeAddress and phone
City tax office (Lafayette Consolidated Government)2701 Moss St., 337-291-8272
Parish tax collector (Sheriff)916 Lafayette St., 337-236-5400
Environmental Quality Division337-291-8500
Compliance Division337-291-8445

A Lafayette homeowner often holds two bills, one from the city and one from the parish, and each office takes payment separately. Tax sale day is the first Wednesday in June, held online.

City tax bills and payment

City tax is billed apart from parish tax. Notices go out from Lafayette Consolidated Government at the end of November and are delinquent after December 31. Interest of 1% per month is added after that, and a penalty begins in February.

The city will not take partial payments, so the whole assessment must be paid in one go. Options:

  • Pay online.
  • Walk in at 2701 Moss Street between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. on weekdays. Cash, check or money order is accepted, and checks go to Lafayette Consolidated Government.
  • Mail payment to P.O. Box 4024-C, Lafayette, LA 70502.

The Sheriff's Office handles parish taxes through its web tax site, which takes e-check and major credit cards for a transaction fee. Before the act of sale, ask your closing agent to confirm both the city and parish bills are current.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The June tax sale and adjudicated property

The joint city and parish tax sale happens online on the first Wednesday in June. The list of properties appears in the local newspaper on the two Sundays before.

When nobody buys a home with unpaid taxes at the sheriff's sale, it becomes adjudicated. It is not owned by the city or parish at that point. The government will not process an application for it until it has been adjudicated three consecutive years. Until the act of sale to an applicant is recorded, the owner can still redeem by paying all taxes, liens and fees to both collectors.

Because 1% interest is added every month and control of the house is at risk, selling early usually costs less than waiting.

Code enforcement

Lafayette Consolidated Government takes property maintenance complaints through its Environmental Quality Division at 337-291-8500. That covers high grass, solid waste, hazardous materials and overgrowth. Run-down structures are handled by the Compliance Division at 337-291-8445.

Vacant and inherited houses draw these complaints fast. Mow the yard and deal with hazards before you list, or choose a buyer who will take the house in its present condition, so a notice does not land in the middle of a contract.

A tax year in Lafayette, step by step

Knowing the calendar helps you decide when to list. Here is how a year runs for a city homeowner.

  1. End of November: Lafayette Consolidated Government mails city notices. The parish bill arrives separately from the Sheriff.
  2. December 31: the last day to pay without penalty on both bills.
  3. January 1 onward: 1% interest per month starts. The city adds a penalty in February.
  4. First Wednesday in June: the online tax sale. The list is published in the local newspaper on the two Sundays before.
  5. After the sale: a house nobody buys is adjudicated, and the owner can redeem until the act of sale to an applicant is recorded.

If you plan to sell in spring, pay or settle the city and parish bills before the sale list is printed. Once a name is on that list, buyers and their title agents will see it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to gather before you list

Closing goes faster when the paperwork is ready. Pull together your most recent city bill and parish bill, plus any notice you have received from the Compliance Division or the Environmental Quality Division. If a lender holds a mortgage, have the payoff contact handy.

Ask the title agent to run a mortgage certificate on your name and check for forgotten liens. Then confirm that the yard is clear of the overgrowth and solid waste that trigger complaints. These steps cost little and keep surprises out of the closing room.

Tax bills can be paid in person at 2701 Moss Street on weekdays, so if a closing date is near and the city balance is still open, you can settle it in a single visit with cash, check or money order. Remember that the city does not accept partial payments.

Two bills, one closing

Because the city and the parish each collect their own tax, a payoff at closing is really two payoffs. The city figure comes from Lafayette Consolidated Government, and the parish figure comes from the Sheriff's tax department. Interest of 1% per month keeps running on any late balance until the day it is paid, so the amounts can differ between the day you order them and the day you sign.

Ask the closing agent to confirm both numbers close to the signing date. If you sold only part of the year, the tax for the year of the sale is a separate matter that the agent will sort out on the settlement statement.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid city and parish taxes are paid from your sale proceeds, so owing money does not prevent a sale. What you need to know is the exact amount owed to each collector, which the title agent can pull before closing.

A Louisiana sale is not complete against outsiders until the deed is filed with the Clerk of Court. Signing is not the finish line. The closing is done once the act of sale is recorded. Our Lafayette Parish clerk guide walks through that step.

A cash purchase skips the buyer's loan approval and appraisal, which helps most when taxes are behind, the house is inherited, a tenant lives there or repairs are needed.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Lafayette property tax due date?

City notices go out at the end of November and are delinquent after December 31. The Sheriff collects the parish bill separately, and its deadline without penalty is also December 31.

Does Lafayette charge interest on late taxes?

Yes. Lafayette Consolidated Government adds 1% interest per month after December 31, and a penalty starts in February. The city does not accept partial payments.

When is the Lafayette tax sale?

It is held online on the first Wednesday in June. The sale list runs in the local newspaper on the two Sundays before.

Is Lafayette prone to flooding?

Lafayette sits on higher prairie terrace and mostly sees local flash flooding, with natural coulees carrying water to the Vermilion River. Check the flood zone for your own lot.

Can I sell a Lafayette house with unpaid city taxes?

Yes. Unpaid city and parish taxes come out of the sale proceeds. A buyer who closes as-is can handle a sale with taxes owed.
